translations.title: 马拉松为什么是 42.195 公里
translations.summary: 马拉松的标准距离是 42.195 公里（26 英里 385 码）。理解这个数字的单位、换算和配速含义，比记住它的历史传说更有用。
translations.body:
## 先给结论

马拉松是一条公路跑项目，标准距离为 **42.195 公里**，也写作 **26 英里 385 码**。这两个表达描述的是同一个距离，只是单位不同。训练计划、配速表和赛道档案都应使用这个标准距离，除非赛事明确采用其他距离或组别。

## 距离从哪里来

现代公路赛事以 World Athletics 的项目定义为准。你不需要记住某一年、某一场比赛的故事，才能理解这个距离；需要记住的是：**42.195 公里是标准值，不是约数**。当一篇训练文章把马拉松写成「42 公里」或「26.2 英里」时，通常只是口语化处理；计算配速时仍应使用 42.195 公里。

英里与公里的换算不是这篇文章的重点，但值得知道两者不能随意混用：按英里配速训练的人，与按公里配速训练的人，看到同一个完赛时间会得到不同的数字。

## 距离如何影响配速

配速是时间除以距离。以 42.195 公里为例：

- 4 小时完赛，平均配速约为 5 分 41 秒/公里。
- 3 小时 30 分完赛，平均配速约为 4 分 59 秒/公里。
- 5 小时完赛，平均配速约为 7 分 07 秒/公里。

这些只是平均值。实际比赛里，起跑拥堵、补给停留、坡度和天气都会让前后半程的配速不同。把平均值当作目标时，要预留这些变量，而不是要求每一公里都一模一样。

需要准确换算时，使用跑地图工具站的[配速计算器](/zh-CN/tools/pace/)，输入距离与时间，分别得到配速和速度。

## 训练上的含义

42.195 公里不是两个半程马拉松简单相加。后半程的糖原、肌肉疲劳、补水节奏和心理波动，都要求你在训练中安排足够长的连续跑，并练习比赛日的补给与装备。具体安排应结合个人基础，不要直接套用他人的周跑量。

如果你想先理解「轻松跑」为何占训练的大部分，可以继续阅读[轻松跑到底是什么强度](/zh-CN/articles/easy-run/)。

## 常见混淆

- **「全马」与「半马」**：半程马拉松是 21.0975 公里，正好是标准马拉松的一半；两者不是同一个项目。
- **赛道距离与 GPS 距离**：手表记录的轨迹可能因信号漂移略长或略短，不能用来否定官方赛道距离。
- **超级马拉松**：超过标准马拉松距离的公路或越野赛事属于另一类项目，不应套用马拉松配速模型。

## 来源与适用范围

本文的距离定义依据 World Athletics 的公路跑项目说明。配速示例为算术换算，不构成训练计划或完赛承诺。核验日期为 2026-10-27。

translations.title: Why the marathon is 42.195 kilometres
translations.summary: The standard marathon distance is 42.195 km (26 miles 385 yards). Understanding the units, conversions and pace implications is more useful than memorising origin stories.
translations.body:
## The short answer

The marathon is a road running event over **42.195 kilometres**, also expressed as **26 miles and 385 yards**. Both describe the same distance in different units. Training plans, pace tables and course profiles should use this standard distance unless an event explicitly offers a different distance or category.

## Where the distance comes from

Modern road events use the World Athletics discipline definition. You do not need to remember a particular year or race story to understand the distance; what matters is that **42.195 km is a standard, not an approximation**. When an article writes "42 km" or "26.2 miles", that is usually shorthand. Pace calculations should still use 42.195 km.

Miles and kilometres should not be mixed casually: runners training by mile pace and runners training by kilometre pace will see different numbers for the same finish time.

## How distance affects pace

Pace is time divided by distance. Over 42.195 km:

- A 4:00 finish averages about 5:41 per kilometre.
- A 3:30 finish averages about 4:59 per kilometre.
- A 5:00 finish averages about 7:07 per kilometre.

These are averages only. In a real race, start congestion, aid-station stops, hills and weather make the first and second halves differ. Treat an average as a target to manage, not a demand that every kilometre be identical.

For accurate conversions, use the [pace calculator](/en/tools/pace/) in RunMap Tools: enter distance and time to get both pace and speed.

## What it means for training

42.195 km is not simply two half marathons added together. Glycogen, muscle fatigue, hydration rhythm and psychological swings in the later stages all argue for enough long continuous runs in training, plus practice with race-day fuelling and equipment. The details depend on your own base; do not copy someone else's weekly volume.

If you want to understand why easy running makes up much of a training week, read [what easy running really means](/en/articles/easy-run/).

## Common confusions

- **Marathon and half marathon**: the half marathon is 21.0975 km, exactly half the standard marathon. They are different events.
- **Course distance and GPS distance**: a watch track can measure slightly long or short because of signal drift. It does not override the official course distance.
- **Ultramarathon**: road or trail events longer than the standard marathon are a different category. Marathon pace models do not automatically apply.

## Sources and scope

The distance definition follows World Athletics' road running discipline description. The pace examples are arithmetic and are not a training plan or a finish-time promise. It was checked on 2026-10-27.

sources.title: Knee pain and other running injuries
claims: NHS advises buying proper running shoes and getting fitted at a running shop, while noting that expensive shoes are not essential.
Unsupportive or worn-out shoes are listed among factors that can contribute to heel pain.
Do not run while in pain; seek medical or physiotherapy advice when pain is severe, persistent or accompanied by swelling.

sources.title: The Association Between Running Injuries and Training Parameters: A Systematic Review
claims: Across 36 studies and 23,047 runners, 26.2% reported a running-related injury.
Evidence linking weekly distance, duration, frequency, intensity or recent changes to injury was conflicting.
The authors caution against recommending one optimal training progression for every runner.

translations.title: 跑步疼痛、负荷与何时求助
translations.summary: 疼痛不是必须忍过去的训练勋章。记录位置、出现方式和负荷变化，先停止或减少加重因素；持续、严重或伴随肿胀的疼痛需要专业评估。
translations.body:
## 疼痛是信息，不是意志测试

跑步中出现疼痛时，先停止或降低强度，观察疼痛是否在继续跑时加重、是否改变步态，以及是否伴随肿胀、无力或关节卡住。NHS 明确建议不要带着疼痛继续跑；恢复后再逐步回到跑步。带痛硬撑不会因为“适应”而自动变成安全训练。

## 记录，而不是猜一个诊断

记录疼痛位置、开始时间、动作（上坡、下坡、加速、久坐后起步）、持续时间和前一天训练量。把“膝盖痛”拆成更具体的时间和动作信息，能帮助你与医生、物理治疗师沟通。本页不根据部位给出诊断，也不把常见名称当成确定病因。

## 负荷变化不是唯一原因

一项纳入 36 项研究、23,047 名跑者的系统综述报告约 26.2% 的跑者发生跑步相关损伤；但每周距离、时长、频率、强度和近期变化与损伤风险的证据互相冲突。作者明确提醒，不应给所有跑者推荐同一个“最佳”训练进度。负荷管理重要，但不能解释所有疼痛。

## 什么时候应该求助

NHS 建议：严重膝痛或肿胀应尽快就医；膝痛持续超过一周，或跟腱疼痛持续两到三周，应找全科医生或物理治疗师；跟腱突然出现尖锐疼痛可能是撕裂，应尽快就医评估。还可以把“无法负重、明显变形、发热、夜间痛醒、持续心悸/胸痛/晕厥”视为不等待自行观察的信号。紧急情况应联系当地急救服务。

## 怎样相对休息

“休息”不等于完全不动。可以暂时减少跑量、避免加重疼痛的速度和坡度，保留无痛的低强度活动；等症状稳定后，先用短而轻松的跑走交替试水，再逐步恢复。NHS 的渐进建议是：同一强度的跑至少重复三到四次，再考虑增加距离或速度。具体计划应由了解你情况的人调整。

## 本站不提供什么

这里不做诊断、不推荐药物、不替代影像或体格检查，也不保证“跑姿/鞋/拉伸”能解决疼痛。疼痛原因可能与既往伤病、骨应力、肌腱、肌肉或其他医学问题有关；需要专业评估时不要拖延。

## 来源与适用范围

疼痛警示和渐进建议参考 NHS 的跑步损伤页面；训练参数与损伤风险的冲突证据参考 Journal of Athletic Training 的系统综述。两者都是一般信息，不构成个体化医疗建议。

translations.title: Running pain, load and when to seek help
translations.summary: Pain is not a training badge to push through. Record where and when it appears and what changed in load; persistent, severe pain or pain with swelling deserves professional assessment.
translations.body:
## Pain is information, not a willpower test

When pain appears during a run, stop or reduce intensity and observe whether it worsens with continued running, changes your gait, or comes with swelling, weakness or a joint that catches. The NHS explicitly advises not running while in pain and returning gradually after recovery. Pushing through pain does not automatically become safe training through “adaptation”.

## Record, do not guess a diagnosis

Record the location, when it began, the movement that brings it on (uphill, downhill, acceleration, first steps after sitting), duration and recent training load. Turning “knee pain” into specific timing and movement information helps a clinician or physiotherapist. This page does not diagnose by body part or treat a common label as a confirmed cause.

## Load change is not the only cause

A systematic review of 36 studies and 23,047 runners reported that about 26.2% had a running-related injury. Evidence linking weekly distance, duration, frequency, intensity or recent changes to injury was conflicting. The authors explicitly caution against one “optimal” progression for every runner. Load matters, but it does not explain every pain.

## When to seek help

NHS advice includes urgent assessment for severe knee pain or swelling; review by a GP or physiotherapist if knee pain persists beyond a week, or for Achilles pain lasting two to three weeks; sudden sharp Achilles pain may be a tear and should be assessed promptly. Other reasons not to wait include inability to bear weight, obvious deformity, fever, pain waking you at night, or persistent palpitations, chest pain or fainting. Use local emergency services for emergencies.

## Relative rest, not total stillness

Rest does not mean doing nothing. Temporarily reduce running volume and avoid the speeds and gradients that provoke pain, while keeping comfortable low-intensity movement. When symptoms settle, test with short, easy run-walk intervals and build gradually. The NHS progression suggestion is to repeat a similar run at least three or four times before increasing distance or pace. A clinician who knows your situation should adjust the plan.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not diagnose, recommend medication, replace imaging or a physical examination, or promise that “form, shoes or stretching” will cure pain. Causes may involve previous injury, bone stress, tendons, muscles or other medical issues. Do not delay professional assessment when it is needed.

## Sources and scope

Pain warnings and gradual-return advice follow the NHS running-injury page; conflicting evidence on training parameters follows a Journal of Athletic Training systematic review. Both are general information, not individual medical advice.

sources.title: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
claims: Generalised anxiety disorder is a common mental health condition involving persistent worry that affects daily life and is difficult to control.
Symptoms can include sleep difficulty, restlessness, irritability, fatigue, tension, stomach problems and palpitations.
Most people feel anxious sometimes; GAD is more likely when anxiety is present most of the time and affects everyday life.
Adults can see a GP or refer themselves to NHS talking therapies for anxiety and depression.

sources.title: Burn-out an occupational phenomenon: International Classification of Diseases
claims: Burn-out is included in ICD-11 as an occupational phenomenon and is not classified as a medical condition.
WHO defines burn-out as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.
The three dimensions are energy depletion or exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism related to one's job, and reduced professional efficacy.
WHO states that burn-out refers specifically to the occupational context and should not be applied to other areas of life.

sources.title: Insomnia
claims: Everyone needs different amounts of sleep.
On average, adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
Insomnia means regularly having problems sleeping and usually improves by changing sleeping habits.
Persistent sleep problems can affect daily life and may need medical advice.

translations.title: 赛前焦虑与训练倦怠：把压力说清楚
translations.summary: 赛前紧张很常见，但持续影响生活的焦虑不是意志问题。训练倦怠也不是正式医学诊断；当疲惫、失眠和表现下降持续时，先减负荷并寻求合适帮助。
translations.body:
## 赛前紧张不等于焦虑症

NHS 指出，焦虑是对压力的常见反应，偶尔紧张并不等于广泛性焦虑障碍（GAD）。GAD 更常见于长期、广泛且难以控制的担忧，并影响日常生活；症状可能包括睡眠困难、坐立不安、易怒、疲劳、肌肉紧张、胃部不适和心悸。

赛前心跳加快、反复检查装备或睡不好，很多跑者都经历过。如果担忧持续数周、影响工作或睡眠，或让你无法正常训练和生活，应该考虑和医生或心理专业人员谈谈；NHS 也允许成年人直接转介谈话治疗。

## 可执行的小动作

与其要求自己“别紧张”，不如把注意力放到可执行的事情上：提前整理装备和路线，按熟悉的流程热身，给自己几句具体的提示（例如“前 5 公里放松”“上坡缩短步幅”），并允许自己紧张。

避免在赛前临时增加咖啡因、补剂或陌生仪式；这些可能放大心悸和焦虑。把担忧写下来、和同伴聊一聊，或使用你熟悉的呼吸/注意力练习，也比反复刷成绩预测更有帮助。

## 训练倦怠不是懒

WHO 把“burn-out”列为职业现象，并明确它不是医学诊断，也不应套用到生活其他领域。跑者常说的“训练倦怠”不是一个正式诊断，可能混合了睡眠不足、能量摄入不足、生活压力、重复训练和疾病等因素。

如果持续疲惫、对训练失去兴趣、表现明显下降、睡眠变差或情绪低落超过一两周，先减少训练量和强度，检查睡眠、饮食和压力，并考虑寻求医疗或心理评估。不要用“再坚持一下”掩盖持续恶化的信号。

## 生活负荷与目标

工作、家庭、照护和经济压力都会影响训练。目标可以调整：把比赛当作体验、缩短距离、推迟比赛或暂时只维持健康，都是合理选择。休息不是失败，也不需要用一次比赛证明自己的价值。

如果训练已经变成持续的自责、隐藏或强迫行为，应认真对待；和可信任的人、医生或心理专业人员讨论，比独自硬撑更安全。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不诊断焦虑、抑郁、进食障碍或过度训练，也不提供心理治疗或药物建议。若你或身边的人有自伤风险、严重绝望或精神危机，请联系当地急救或危机干预服务，不要等待训练计划调整。

## 来源与适用范围

焦虑症状和求助路径参考 NHS 的广泛性焦虑障碍页面；倦怠定义参考 WHO 的 ICD-11 说明；睡眠与恢复原则参考本站睡眠文章及其来源。本文只提供一般识别和行动框架，不替代专业评估。

translations.title: Race anxiety and training burnout: name the pressure
translations.summary: Pre-race nerves are common, but anxiety that persistently affects daily life is not a character flaw. Training burnout is not a formal diagnosis; when exhaustion, poor sleep and declining performance persist, reduce load and seek appropriate help.
translations.body:
## Pre-race nerves are not automatically an anxiety disorder

The NHS notes that anxiety is a common response to stress and that occasional worry does not mean generalised anxiety disorder (GAD). GAD is more likely when worry is widespread, persistent and difficult to control, and affects daily life. Symptoms can include sleep difficulty, restlessness, irritability, fatigue, muscle tension, stomach problems and palpitations.

A faster heartbeat, repeated kit checks or poor sleep before a race are familiar to many runners. If worry lasts for weeks, affects work or sleep, or makes normal training and life difficult, consider talking to a clinician or mental-health professional. Adults in the UK can also refer themselves to NHS talking therapies.

## Small actions that help

Rather than telling yourself to “just stop worrying”, put attention on actions: prepare kit and route in advance, use a familiar warm-up, choose a few specific cues (“relax the first 5 km”, “shorten the stride uphill”), and allow yourself to feel nervous.

Avoid adding new caffeine, supplements or rituals on race day; they can amplify palpitations and anxiety. Writing worries down, talking to a friend, or using a familiar breathing or attention practice is usually more useful than repeatedly refreshing race predictions.

## Training burnout is not laziness

WHO lists “burn-out” as an occupational phenomenon and states that it is not classified as a medical condition and should not be applied to other areas of life. Runners' “training burnout” is not a formal diagnosis; it may combine insufficient sleep, low energy intake, life stress, repetitive training and illness.

If persistent exhaustion, loss of interest, a clear performance drop, worsening sleep or low mood lasts more than a week or two, reduce training volume and intensity, review sleep, food and stress, and consider medical or psychological assessment. Do not use “push through” to mask worsening signals.

## Life load and goals

Work, family, caregiving and financial stress all affect training. Goals can change: treating a race as an experience, shortening the distance, deferring it, or simply maintaining health for a while are all legitimate choices. Rest is not failure, and one race does not define your worth.

If training has become persistent self-criticism, secrecy or compulsion, take it seriously. Talking with someone you trust, a clinician or a mental-health professional is safer than struggling alone.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not diagnose anxiety, depression, eating disorders or overtraining, and does not provide psychotherapy or medication advice. If you or someone else is at risk of self-harm, severely hopeless or in a mental-health crisis, contact local emergency or crisis services rather than waiting to adjust a training plan.

## Sources and scope

Anxiety symptoms and help pathways follow the NHS generalised anxiety disorder page; the definition of burnout follows WHO's ICD-11 note; sleep and recovery principles follow this site's sleep article and its sources. This page offers a general recognition and action framework, not a substitute for professional assessment.

sources.title: Insomnia
claims: Everyone needs different amounts of sleep.
On average, adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
Insomnia means regularly having problems sleeping and usually improves by changing sleeping habits.
Persistent sleep problems can affect daily life and may need medical advice.

translations.title: 恢复日该休息还是动一动
translations.summary: 跑步训练中的恢复日不是空白，而是让适应真正发生的部分。选择完全休息还是低强度活动，取决于疲劳来源、睡眠和身体信号。
translations.body:
## 恢复也是训练

训练给身体一个刺激，恢复期才发生适应。把恢复日理解成「没有训练」容易导致两个极端：要么完全忽略它，继续加量；要么把它当成必须彻底静止的教条。更实用的做法是：**先确认自己在恢复什么，再选择休息方式**。

一次普通轻松跑后的恢复需求，和一场马拉松或高山越野后的恢复需求完全不同；睡眠不足带来的疲劳，也不能靠一次慢跑解决。

## 完全休息什么时候更合适

以下情况更适合安排完全休息或低活动量的一天：

- 连续多日训练后，主观疲劳明显升高，轻松跑也不轻松。
- 睡眠不足，白天注意力或情绪受到明显影响。
- 出现不同于普通肌肉酸痛的疼痛，例如局部刺痛、关节肿胀或走路时加重。
- 刚完成比赛或超长距离训练，组织修复需要更长时间。
- 生病、发热或正在从感染中恢复。

疼痛不等于「练到了」。如果疼痛持续、夜间加重或影响日常行走，应停止训练并寻求医疗建议，而不是用恢复日硬扛。

## 主动恢复怎样才算「主动」

主动恢复指的是低强度、低负担的活动，例如轻松步行、非常轻松的慢跑、游泳或骑车。判断标准仍然是谈话测试：能轻松说完整句子，结束后不增加明显疲劳。它不应变成一次隐藏的质量课。

如果主动恢复让你第二天更累，那就说明它不轻。恢复日不需要完成距离目标，也不需要为「没跑够」补偿。

## 睡眠是恢复的核心变量

NHS 指出，每个人需要的睡眠量不同，大多数成年人需要 7 至 9 小时。睡眠是恢复的重要背景变量；如果连续几天变差，先降低训练量并观察，而不是继续叠加恢复设备或补剂。

改善睡眠没有万能技巧。固定起床时间、减少睡前刺激、把高强度训练与入睡时间拉开，都是常见方向；如果失眠持续并影响白天功能，应咨询医生，而不是依赖补剂或酒精。

## 记录什么

恢复日适合记录几项简单信息，帮助你看趋势，而不是被单日数字牵着走：

- 睡眠时长与主观质量。
- 起床后的疲劳感，以及是否有异常疼痛。
- 静息心率或主观状态（如果有长期记录习惯）。
- 当天训练内容与感受。
- 食欲、情绪和注意力。

穿戴设备可以提供参考，但不能诊断过度训练或恢复不足。单次心率异常可能来自咖啡、酒精、炎热或测量误差；连续多日的趋势更有意义。

## 赛后恢复的粗略框架

马拉松或超长越野后，恢复时间通常以周计，而不是以天计。可以先恢复日常步行和睡眠，再逐步加入轻松跑；在疼痛消失、走路正常、睡眠稳定之前，不急于回到质量课。具体时间因人和比赛难度而异，本文不给固定天数。

如果你在恢复期出现持续心悸、胸痛、晕厥、异常肿胀或伤口不愈，应及时就医，不要只靠调整训练解决。

## 来源与适用范围

本文关于睡眠时长与个体差异的表述依据 NHS 的失眠与睡眠说明。本文提供一般恢复原则，不构成医疗诊断或个体化治疗建议。核验日期为 2026-10-27。

translations.title: Should a recovery day be rest or easy movement?
translations.summary: In running, a recovery day is not a blank space in the plan; it is when adaptation happens. Choose full rest or low-intensity movement based on the source of fatigue, sleep and your body's signals.
translations.body:
## Recovery is training

Training provides a stimulus; adaptation happens during recovery. Treating a recovery day as "no training" encourages two extremes: ignoring it and adding more load, or turning it into a rule that you must lie completely still. A more useful approach is to ask **what you are recovering from**, then choose the recovery method.

The recovery needed after an ordinary easy run is nothing like the recovery needed after a marathon or a high-mountain ultra. Fatigue caused by poor sleep will not be fixed by an easy jog either.

## When full rest is the better choice

Consider a full rest day or very low activity when:

- Perceived fatigue is clearly elevated after several consecutive days, and even an easy run feels hard.
- Sleep has been poor and attention or mood is noticeably affected during the day.
- You have pain that differs from ordinary muscle soreness, such as local sharp pain, joint swelling or pain that worsens when walking.
- You have just finished a race or a very long training session and tissue repair needs more time.
- You are ill, feverish or recovering from an infection.

Pain does not mean "the training worked". If pain persists, worsens at night or changes how you walk, stop training and seek medical advice rather than pushing through a recovery day.

## What counts as active recovery

Active recovery means low-intensity, low-load movement: an easy walk, a very gentle jog, swimming or cycling. The talk test still applies: you can speak in full sentences easily and do not finish noticeably more tired. It should not become a hidden quality session.

If active recovery leaves you more tired the next day, it was not easy. A recovery day does not require a distance target, and there is nothing to "make up" for not running.

## Sleep is a core recovery variable

The NHS notes that everyone needs different amounts of sleep and that most adults need 7 to 9 hours. Sleep is an important recovery context; if it deteriorates for several days, reduce training load and observe rather than stacking more recovery gadgets or supplements on top.

There is no universal sleep trick. A consistent wake time, less stimulation before bed and separating hard training from bedtime are common directions. If insomnia persists and affects daytime function, consult a doctor rather than relying on supplements or alcohol.

## What to record

A recovery day is a good time to note a few simple signals and look at trends rather than letting one day's number dictate everything:

- Sleep duration and perceived quality.
- Morning fatigue and any unusual pain.
- Resting heart rate or subjective state, if you already track them over time.
- The day's training and how it felt.
- Appetite, mood and attention.

Wearables can offer context but cannot diagnose overtraining or under-recovery. A single odd heart-rate reading may come from caffeine, alcohol, heat or measurement error; a trend over several days is more meaningful.

## A rough framework after a race

Recovery after a marathon or a long mountain ultra is usually measured in weeks, not days. Start by restoring daily walking and sleep, then add easy running gradually. Do not rush back to quality sessions until pain has settled, walking is normal and sleep is stable. Timelines vary with the person and the race, so this article gives no fixed number of days.

Seek medical care for persistent palpitations, chest pain, fainting, unusual swelling or a wound that does not heal; do not treat these by adjusting training alone.

## Sources and scope

The statements about sleep duration and individual variation follow the NHS information on insomnia and sleep. This article offers general recovery principles, not medical diagnosis or individual treatment. It was checked on 2026-10-27.

sources.title: Knee pain and other running injuries
claims: NHS advises buying proper running shoes and getting fitted at a running shop, while noting that expensive shoes are not essential.
Unsupportive or worn-out shoes are listed among factors that can contribute to heel pain.
Do not run while in pain; seek medical or physiotherapy advice when pain is severe, persistent or accompanied by swelling.

sources.title: Get running with Couch to 5K
claims: Couch to 5K schedules three runs a week with rest days between, over nine weeks or longer.
It starts with one-minute runs and 1.5-minute walks and builds toward 30 minutes of continuous running.
The NHS advises going at your own pace and speaking to a GP if you are worried about your health before starting.

translations.title: 中断后怎样恢复跑步：从可重复的小剂量开始
translations.summary: 中断训练后，恢复跑步的目标是重新建立可重复的负荷，而不是一次补回损失。先从无痛步行和跑走交替开始，逐步增加。
translations.body:
## 先判断你在从哪里回来

恢复跑步的起点可能是感冒、旅行、工作繁忙、一次疼痛，或较长时间的停训。不同原因需要不同条件：如果疼痛仍在、走路异常、肿胀或夜间痛醒，不应直接恢复跑步；先寻求医疗或物理治疗评估。NHS 明确建议不要带痛跑步。

## 从走路和跑走交替开始

如果日常走路已经无痛且稳定，可以用短时间跑走交替作为第一周：短跑段、足够长的步行恢复，总时间控制在轻松范围。NHS 的 Couch to 5K 也用一分钟跑加一分半走作为起点，并安排每周三次、之间休息。具体比例应按你的反应调整。

## 同一剂量重复几次

NHS 的渐进建议是同一强度的跑至少重复三到四次，再考虑增加距离或速度。中断越久，重复次数越重要；不要因为一次感觉良好就连续加码。记录跑后当天和第二天的情况：疼痛、疲劳、睡眠和走路是否正常。

## 什么时候暂停

如果跑步让疼痛加重、改变步态、出现新的肿胀或持续到第二天，停止并回到无痛活动；症状持续或反复时寻求专业评估。发热、胸痛、晕厥或异常气短不是“慢慢适应”的对象，应停止运动并及时就医。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不给个体化复跑计划或伤病诊断，也不保证某种进度适合你的情况。术后、骨应力损伤、心血管问题或孕产恢复等情境需要相应专业人员指导，不能只靠网页决定。

## 来源与适用范围

疼痛警示和渐进建议参考 NHS 的跑步损伤页面；跑走交替结构参考 NHS Couch to 5K。本文是一般恢复框架，不是医疗处方。

translations.title: Returning to running after a break: start with repeatable small doses
translations.summary: After a break, the goal is to rebuild repeatable load, not to make up lost training in one session. Start with pain-free walking and run-walk intervals, then progress gradually.
translations.body:
## First identify what you are returning from

The starting point might be a cold, travel, a busy period, a pain episode or a long layoff. Different causes need different conditions: do not resume running while pain persists, walking is abnormal, swelling is present or pain wakes you at night; seek medical or physiotherapy assessment first. The NHS explicitly advises not running while in pain.

## Start with walking and run-walk

If everyday walking is pain-free and stable, use short run-walk intervals for the first week: brief running, generous walking recovery and an easy total time. NHS Couch to 5K also starts with one-minute runs and 1.5-minute walks, three times a week with rest between. Adjust the ratio to your response.

## Repeat the same dose several times

NHS progression advice is to repeat a similar run at least three or four times before increasing distance or pace. The longer the break, the more those repeats matter; do not add more just because one session felt good. Record the rest of the day and the next day: pain, fatigue, sleep and normal walking.

## When to pause

If running worsens pain, changes your gait, causes new swelling or persists into the next day, stop and return to pain-free activity; seek professional assessment if symptoms persist or recur. Fever, chest pain, fainting or unusual breathlessness are not things to “adapt to”; stop and seek medical help.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not give an individual return-to-running plan or diagnose an injury, and does not promise that a progression suits you. Post-surgical recovery, bone-stress injury, cardiovascular conditions and postpartum return need guidance from the relevant professional, not a web page alone.

## Sources and scope

Pain warnings and progression follow the NHS running-injury page; the run-walk structure follows NHS Couch to 5K. This is a general recovery framework, not a medical prescription.

sources.title: Heat Cramps, Exhaustion, Stroke
claims: Heat exhaustion can cause heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache and fainting.
Heat stroke is an emergency with confusion, slurred speech, very high body temperature, rapid pulse and possible loss of consciousness.
Heat stroke requires emergency services; call emergency services first and cool the person while waiting.

sources.title: Hike Smart
claims: Leave a trip plan with a trusted person including route, contacts, arrival and return times, and companions.
Mobile coverage may be absent; consider a locator beacon and conserve battery.
Check the weather, prepare for lightning and flash flooding, and keep a Plan B.

Carry a map, compass, headlamp with spare batteries, whistle, first aid and extra layers.

translations.title: 路线、天气与夜间安全：跑步前的检查清单
translations.summary: GPX 只描述线路几何，不说明封路、补给、手机信号或天气风险。出发前留下行程、查看天气、带好照明和水，并准备撤退方案。
translations.body:
## 路线文件不等于安全路线

GPX 或地图只能记录线路几何，部分文件还会带高程、时间或路点；它们不能告诉你今天是否封路、是否有水源、手机是否有信号、天黑后能否通行，也不能代替对交通、天气和地形的判断。把路线文件当作计划底图，把赛事或土地管理方的当届公告当作事实来源。

## 出发前留下计划

美国国家公园管理局建议把路线、联系人、预计到达和返回时间、同行者告诉一个不与你同行的可信的人。手机上留一份离线地图和备份联系方式；如果进入无信号区域，考虑定位信标并节省电池。不要假设“有人知道我去哪”就够了，时间和路线要具体。

## 天气与高温

出发前查看预报和预警，准备闪电、暴雨、积水或高温的替代方案。高温下出现大量出汗、虚弱、头晕、恶心、头痛或昏厥，可能是热衰竭；如果呕吐、症状加重或持续超过一小时，应降温并寻求医疗帮助；出现意识混乱、言语不清、极高体温、强而快的脉搏或失去意识，可能是热射病，应立即呼叫当地急救，不要只让当事人“再坚持一下”。热射病不是靠继续跑步或自行补水处理的。

## 夜间与可见度

夜间要有头灯和备用电池，尽量选择已知路线和可撤退节点；穿反光或高可见度衣物，告知同行者。独自夜跑时，把“按时报平安”设为硬性节点，而不是可选项。不要为了完成配速在视线不足时下技术坡。

## 水、装备与同行

国家公园管理局建议根据条件携带足够饮水，并在水用掉一半时考虑折返；越野或长距离还应携带地图/指南针、头灯、哨子、急救包、额外保暖和基础维修。GPS 可能失效，不能只依赖一块手表或手机。同行、缩短路线和提前折返都是有效的安全决策。

## GPX 的边界

本页不提供某条路线的实时封路、补给、救援或通行授权信息。不同土地管理方有不同规则，私人土地和保护区可能禁止进入。使用任何轨迹前，先确认来源许可、线路是否开放、当天天气和当地紧急电话。

## 来源与适用范围

高温识别参考美国国家气象局；行程计划、天气和导航参考美国国家公园管理局的 Hike Smart 与 Hiking Safety Tips。急救电话与医疗处置因国家/地区而异，本页不替代当地救援培训。

translations.title: Route, weather and night safety: a pre-run checklist
translations.summary: A GPX describes route geometry, not closures, water, phone coverage or weather risk. Leave a trip plan, check the weather, carry light and water, and prepare an escape option.
translations.body:
## A route file is not a safe route

A GPX or map records route geometry, and some files also carry elevation, timestamps or waypoints. It does not tell you whether a road is closed today, whether water is available, whether your phone has coverage, whether the ground is passable after dark, or whether traffic, weather and terrain make the plan sensible. Treat the route file as a planning base and the current race or land-manager notice as the source of truth.

## Leave a trip plan

The U.S. National Park Service recommends giving a trusted person who is not on the trip the route, contacts, expected arrival and return times and companions. Keep an offline map and backup contact details on your phone; in areas without coverage, consider a locator beacon and conserve battery. “Someone knows I went running” is not enough if the route and timing are vague.

## Weather and heat

Check the forecast and warnings before leaving, and prepare alternatives for lightning, heavy rain, flooding or heat. Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache or fainting can indicate heat exhaustion; if there is vomiting, worsening symptoms or symptoms lasting over an hour, cool the person and seek medical help. Confusion, slurred speech, very high body temperature, a rapid strong pulse or loss of consciousness can indicate heat stroke: call local emergency services immediately and do not simply tell the person to keep going. Heat stroke is not managed by continuing to run or drinking water on your own.

## Night and visibility

Use a headlamp with spare batteries at night, prefer known routes with escape points, wear reflective or high-visibility clothing and tell someone your plan. For solo night runs, make “check in on time” a firm checkpoint, not an option. Do not descend technical terrain in poor visibility just to hit a pace target.

## Water, kit and company

The National Park Service recommends carrying enough water for the conditions and considering turning back when half is gone. For trails and long runs, also carry a map/compass, headlamp, whistle, first aid, extra warmth and basic repair kit. GPS can fail; do not rely only on a watch or phone. Running with someone, shortening the route and turning around early are valid safety decisions.

## The limits of a GPX

This page does not provide live closure, aid, rescue or access-authorisation information for a specific route. Land-manager rules differ, and private land or protected areas may be closed. Before using any track, confirm its licence, whether the route is open, the day's weather and the local emergency number.

## Sources and scope

Heat recognition follows the U.S. National Weather Service; trip planning, weather and navigation follow the U.S. National Park Service Hike Smart and Hiking Safety Tips pages. Emergency numbers and medical care vary by country; this page does not replace local rescue training.

sources.title: Older Adult Activity: An Overview
claims: Adults aged 65 and older need aerobic, muscle-strengthening and balance activities each week.
The aerobic target is at least 150 minutes at moderate intensity, 75 minutes at vigorous intensity, or an equivalent combination.
Older adults need at least two days of muscle-strengthening activity and activities that improve balance.
People benefit from physical activity throughout life, including as they age.

sources.title: Chronic Conditions & Disabilities Activity
claims: Adults with chronic health conditions or disabilities can be physically active and gain important health benefits.
Adults with chronic conditions or disabilities who are able should get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity a week and at least two days of muscle-strengthening activity.
Some physical activity is better than none; people should be as active as they are able.
Regular activity can improve function, sleep, mental health and cardiovascular health for people with chronic conditions.

sources.title: Tips for Maintaining Healthy Weight
claims: Healthy pregnant or postpartum women need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week.
Weight is influenced by factors including sleep, age, genes and medications.
People who are physically active can still gain weight if they take in more calories than they use.
A health care provider is the best person to ask whether illnesses or medications are contributing to weight gain or making weight loss difficult.

sources.title: Weight Gain During Pregnancy
claims: Physical activity is healthy and safe for most pregnant women.
Pregnant women should talk to their health care provider about any physical activity restrictions.

translations.title: 不同人生阶段的跑步：女性、年长跑者与慢性病
translations.summary: 多数成年人的有氧和力量指南相同，但孕期产后、年长跑者和慢性病跑者需要把个体条件放进计划。先保证安全与可持续，再谈配速和成绩。
translations.body:
## 指南适用于多数成年人

CDC 建议成年人每周至少 150 分钟中等强度有氧活动，或等量的高强度活动，并每周至少两天进行覆盖主要肌群的力量训练。活动可以分散到一周内完成，少量活动也比完全不活动好。

这些是一般人群的底线，不是比赛训练计划。跑步只是有氧活动的一种；如果你刚开始、刚恢复或正在处理健康问题，先以能稳定重复的量为起点，再逐渐增加。

## 女性、孕期与产后

女性跑者和男性遵循相同的基本有氧与力量建议。孕期和产后是特殊阶段：CDC 指出，身体活动对大多数孕妇是健康且安全的，健康孕妇和产后女性每周至少 150 分钟中等强度活动；但每个人都应和产检或产后医生讨论活动限制。

产后恢复速度差异很大，不应被社交媒体上的“快速回归”绑架。骨盆底症状、持续出血、伤口问题、头晕或疼痛应寻求医疗评估；恢复跑步前，先确认日常活动和力量基础是否稳定。

## 年长跑者

CDC 对 65 岁及以上成年人的建议包括有氧、力量以及改善平衡的活动。年龄本身不是停止跑步的理由，但平衡能力、骨密度、药物、既往伤病和恢复速度需要纳入安排。

年长跑者更需要重视力量、平衡和渐进负荷，而不是和别人比较配速。出现跌倒、胸闷、异常气短、头晕或新发疼痛时，应停止运动并寻求医疗建议。

## 慢性病与用药

CDC 指出，有慢性健康问题或残障的成年人可以活动，并能获得健康收益；在能力允许时，目标同样是每周至少 150 分钟中等强度有氧活动和至少两天力量训练，少量活动也有价值。

具体安排要结合疾病、药物和当天状态。例如，部分药物会影响心率、体温调节或血糖；高温、脱水和感染会让风险上升。与熟悉你病情的医生或运动专业人士讨论更适合的强度和监测方式，不要自行调整药物。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不诊断疾病、不提供孕期或慢性病的个体化运动处方，也不替代产检、心内科、内分泌科或其他专科随访。胸痛、晕厥、严重气短、意识改变、持续出血或明显异常时，应优先寻求紧急医疗帮助。

## 来源与适用范围

成人、年长者和慢性病活动建议参考 CDC 的成人、老年人和慢性病活动页面；孕期活动与体重信息参考 CDC 的孕期页面。本文只提供一般原则，具体限制应由了解你健康状况的专业人员判断。

translations.title: Running across life: women, older runners and chronic conditions
translations.summary: Most adults share the same aerobic and strength targets, but pregnancy and postpartum, older age and chronic conditions require individual context. Build safety and consistency before pace and performance.
translations.body:
## The guidelines apply to most adults

The CDC recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity a week, or an equivalent amount of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week. Activity can be spread across the week, and some activity is better than none.

These are population minimums, not race plans. Running is one form of aerobic activity. If you are starting, returning or managing a health issue, begin with an amount you can repeat consistently and build from there.

## Women, pregnancy and postpartum

Women runners follow the same basic aerobic and strength guidance as men. Pregnancy and postpartum are special phases: the CDC states that physical activity is healthy and safe for most pregnant women, and healthy pregnant or postpartum women need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week. Each person should discuss activity restrictions with their maternity or postpartum clinician.

Postpartum recovery varies widely and should not be rushed to match social-media timelines. Pelvic-floor symptoms, persistent bleeding, wound problems, dizziness or pain deserve medical assessment. Before returning to running, check that daily activity and strength foundations are stable.

## Older runners

CDC guidance for adults 65 and older includes aerobic activity, muscle strengthening and activities that improve balance. Age alone is not a reason to stop running, but balance, bone health, medication, previous injury and recovery speed belong in the plan.

Older runners benefit more from strength, balance and gradual loading than from comparing pace with younger runners. Stop and seek medical advice for falls, chest symptoms, unusual breathlessness, dizziness or new pain.

## Chronic conditions and medication

The CDC notes that adults with chronic health conditions or disabilities can be active and gain health benefits. When able, the target is still at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week plus two days of muscle strengthening; some activity is better than none.

The details depend on the condition, medication and day-to-day state. Some medicines affect heart rate, temperature regulation or blood glucose; heat, dehydration and infection can raise risk. Discuss appropriate intensity and monitoring with a clinician who knows your condition, and do not change medication on your own.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not diagnose disease, prescribe individual exercise for pregnancy or chronic conditions, or replace maternity, cardiology, endocrinology or other specialist care. Chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, altered consciousness, persistent bleeding or marked deterioration need urgent medical help.

## Sources and scope

Adult, older-adult and chronic-condition guidance follows CDC activity pages; pregnancy activity and weight information follows CDC maternal-health guidance. This page provides general principles; restrictions should be judged by a professional who knows your health situation.

translations.title: 跑步文化：礼仪、纪录与如何读研究
translations.summary: 赛事礼仪是参赛的一部分，纪录有认证和条件，研究结论也有边界。把规则、证据和装备叙事分开看，比追逐一个“最快”故事更接近真实。
translations.body:
## 赛事礼仪不是客套

比赛规则因赛事而异。以波士顿马拉松为例，官方规则明确号码布不可转让，参赛者不得让未注册的人陪跑任何一段，耳机使用要以能保持对周围环境的警觉为前提，专业、轮椅和残障组还有更严格限制；所有参赛者还需遵守赛事行为准则。

这些规则的核心是安全、公平和对其他跑者的尊重。报名前读一遍赛事规则，不在赛道中间突然停下、不横穿、不替跑、不把补给垃圾扔在赛道上；不同比赛对耳机、配速员和补给的规定不同，不要用一场比赛的习惯套到另一场。

## 纪录与赛道条件

World Athletics 按项目公布世界纪录，并标注待批准的纪录；公路纪录还区分混合性别和女子单独出发的比赛。纪录是管理机构的认证，不只是“某个最快时间”的传说。

比较成绩时，要看赛道认证、海拔变化、天气、起跑条件和纪录类别。马拉松距离固定为 42.195 公里，但不同赛道的难度和条件差异很大；把两个不同比赛的完赛时间直接比较，很容易得出错误结论。

## 怎样读跑步研究

一项系统综述汇总了 36 项研究、23,047 名跑者，报告约 26.2% 的人发生过跑步相关伤病；但周跑量、频率、强度或近期变化与伤病之间的关系并不一致，作者也提醒不要给所有人推荐同一种“最佳增量”。

读研究时先看研究设计、样本量、人群、测量方法和作者承认的限制。观察性研究能提示关联，但不能证明因果；一项小样本研究也不足以推翻长期实践。把结论放回证据整体，而不是用一条标题决定训练。

## 装备与技术叙事

跑鞋、碳板、手表和补剂的市场叙事往往把复杂表现归因于单一产品。生理学综述提醒，马拉松表现是生理、技术和认知等多因素共同作用的结果；VO2max、乳酸阈和跑步经济性等指标也受测试方法影响，不能混用。

装备可以帮助舒适、安全或效率，但没有一件产品能替代训练、恢复和个体适应。看到“提升百分之几”的宣传时，先问研究人群、对照条件、资助来源和实际意义。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不提供官方纪录的最终裁定、赛事规则解释或装备推荐。具体规则以赛事组委会为准，纪录以 World Athletics 公布为准；研究方法问题应参考原始论文和统计方法，而不是只看二手摘要。

## 来源与适用范围

赛事礼仪参考波士顿马拉松官方规则；纪录分类参考 World Athletics 纪录页面；跑步伤病证据参考系统综述；表现多因素与测试差异参考生理学综述；马拉松距离参考 World Athletics 项目说明。本文是阅读框架，不替代官方规则或原始研究。

translations.title: Running culture: etiquette, records and reading research
translations.summary: Race etiquette is part of taking part, records have ratification and conditions, and research has limits. Keeping rules, evidence and gear narratives separate gets closer to reality than chasing a single “fastest” story.
translations.body:
## Race etiquette is not decoration

Rules differ by event. The Boston Marathon rules, for example, state that bibs are non-transferable, participants may not run with anyone not registered as an official participant on any part of the course, headphone use must leave runners aware of their surroundings, and professional, wheelchair and para athletics divisions have stricter limits. All participants must also follow the event code of conduct.

The purpose is safety, fairness and respect for other runners. Read the rules before entering; do not stop suddenly in the middle of the course, cut across others, run with someone else's bib or drop gel wrappers on the course. Headphone, pacer and aid rules vary between races, so do not carry one event's habits into another.

## Records and course conditions

World Athletics publishes world records by event and marks records that are pending ratification; road-running tables also distinguish mixed-gender and women-only races. A record is a governing-body recognition, not simply a legendary “fastest time”.

When comparing performances, consider course certification, elevation change, weather, start conditions and record category. The marathon is fixed at 42.195 km, but course difficulty and conditions vary enormously; comparing two finish times without context easily produces the wrong conclusion.

## How to read running research

A systematic review pooled 36 studies and 23,047 runners and reported that about 26.2% had a running-related injury. Yet the evidence linking weekly distance, frequency, intensity or recent changes to injury was inconsistent, and the authors cautioned against recommending one “optimal progression” for everyone.

When reading a study, start with the design, sample size, population, measurements and the limitations the authors acknowledge. Observational studies can show associations but not prove causation; one small study should not overturn long-term practice. Put the result into the wider evidence base rather than letting one headline dictate training.

## Gear and technology narratives

Shoe, plate, watch and supplement marketing often attributes complex performance to a single product. A physiology review reminds us that marathon performance is multi-factorial, involving physiological, technological and cognitive determinants; VO2max, lactate threshold and running economy are also protocol-dependent and should not be treated as interchangeable measurements.

Gear can improve comfort, safety or efficiency, but no product replaces training, recovery and individual adaptation. When a claim promises a percentage improvement, ask about the study population, comparison conditions, funding and practical meaning.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not issue final record rulings, interpret a race's rules for you or recommend gear. Event rules belong to the organiser, records belong to World Athletics, and research questions belong with the original papers and statistical methods rather than second-hand summaries.

## Sources and scope

Race etiquette follows the official Boston Marathon rules; record categories follow the World Athletics records page; running-injury evidence follows a systematic review; multi-factor performance and measurement differences follow a physiology review; marathon distance follows World Athletics event information. This is a reading framework, not a substitute for official rules or original research.

sources.title: Influence of stride frequency and length on running mechanics: a systematic review
claims: Across the reviewed studies, higher stride rate at a fixed speed reduced vertical centre-of-mass excursion, ground reaction force and joint energy absorption.
The review concluded that a higher stride rate may reduce several biomechanical factors associated with running injury.
The included studies were small and methodologically varied, so they do not establish a universal target cadence.

sources.title: Biomechanics and Physiology of Uphill and Downhill Running
claims: Uphill running has a higher step frequency, shorter swing and aerial phase, and greater duty factor than level running.
Downhill running has longer aerial time, lower step frequency and more rear-foot striking than level running.
Downhill running emphasises eccentric work and energy dissipation; uphill running requires greater muscular work, particularly at the hip.

sources.title: Surface effects on kinematics, kinetics and stiffness of habitual rearfoot strikers during running
claims: A small cross-sectional study of 30 male rear-foot strikers found no significant differences in several joint-motion and loading variables across artificial grass, rubber and concrete.
Concrete reduced braking and mediolateral force but increased ankle moments and frontal-plane hip and knee moments.
The authors suggest harder surfaces may increase overuse risk for rear-foot strikers, but the evidence is limited.

sources.title: How to Measure Physical Activity Intensity
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
claims: A person doing moderate-intensity aerobic activity can talk, but not sing, during the activity.
A person doing vigorous-intensity aerobic activity cannot say more than a few words without pausing for a breath.
The talk test is a rule-of-thumb method for estimating aerobic intensity.

translations.title: 跑步技术：步频、步幅、呼吸与上下坡的判断框架
translations.summary: 步频没有唯一正确数字；步幅会随速度变化，呼吸也不该被固定节拍绑住。用少量变量做实验，结合上下坡和路面差异，比追求一个“标准跑姿”更可靠。
translations.body:
## 先观察，再调整

跑步技术不是一个固定姿势。步频、步幅、触地方式和摆臂会随速度、坡度、疲劳和路面变化。与其追求一个看起来“标准”的动作，不如先记录自己在不同条件下的自然节奏，再决定是否需要小改动。

## 步频不是 180 的考试

系统综述发现，在固定速度下提高步频通常会减小身体重心的垂直起伏、地面反作用力和关节能量吸收；这些是与部分跑步损伤相关的生物力学因素。但纳入研究样本较小、方法各异，不能推出“所有人都应该 180 步/分”的结论。把 180 当作参考值，而不是目标值。

更实用的做法是：在轻松跑中数 30 秒步数，连续记录几次，观察疲劳、速度和坡度下的变化。如果你想尝试提高步频，一次只改 5% 左右，保持速度不变，先做两三周，再评估是否更舒适；出现疼痛就停止实验。

## 呼吸节奏不是固定节拍

呼吸会随速度、坡度、疲劳和个人习惯变化，不存在所有人都必须遵循的“三步一吸、两步一呼”。刻意套用固定节拍，可能让肩颈更紧张，反而增加不必要的努力。用谈话测试判断强度更实用：轻松跑应当能说完整句子；如果只能说几个词，说明强度已经偏高，先降速或缩短步幅。

鼻吸口呼、口吸口呼都可以，关键是满足通气需求。没有必要为了“更专业”强迫自己只用鼻子呼吸。若在轻松强度下仍明显气短，或伴随胸闷、喘鸣、头晕，应停止运动并寻求医疗建议。

## 步幅主要由速度决定

步幅不是单独“拉大”的技术指标。速度提高时，步频和步幅通常都会增加；刻意跨大步可能让落地点更靠前，增加制动力和关节负担。先决定要跑的速度，再让步幅自然匹配，而不是用跨大步来追求速度。

## 上坡和下坡不是同一种跑法

研究显示，上坡时步频通常升高，腾空时间缩短，身体更依赖髋部发力；下坡时腾空时间变长、步频降低，离心负荷增加。上坡可以缩短步幅、保持轻松呼吸；下坡则要控制速度，避免为了“放快”而失去落地控制。没有必要把平路节奏原样搬到坡上。

## 路面的影响有限但真实

一项小样本研究比较了人工草、橡胶和混凝土，发现多数关节运动和负荷指标没有显著差异，但混凝土上的踝关节力矩和额状面髋膝力矩更高。单次研究不能给出通用结论，但提醒我们：路面更硬、疲劳累积时，先降低强度并观察身体反应，而不是靠意志硬撑。

## 本站不提供什么

这里不提供个体化跑姿诊断、伤病治疗或“纠正所有跑者”的处方。疼痛、持续不适或既往伤病，应找合格的医疗或运动专业人士评估。技术调整也不能替代睡眠、负荷管理和恢复。

## 来源与适用范围

步频与负荷的关系参考 Sports Health 的系统综述；上下坡差异参考 Sports Medicine 的综述；路面差异参考 PLOS ONE 的小样本研究；呼吸与强度判断参考 CDC 的谈话测试。研究结论有样本和设计限制，本页只把它们转化为可观察的实践框架。

translations.title: Running technique: cadence, stride length, breathing and hills
translations.summary: There is no single correct cadence, stride length changes with speed, and breathing should not be locked to a fixed beat. Small experiments, hill-specific adjustments and surface awareness are more useful than chasing one “ideal” form.
translations.body:
## Observe before changing

Running technique is not one fixed posture. Cadence, stride length, foot strike and arm swing change with speed, gradient, fatigue and surface. Before chasing a “standard” form, record your natural rhythm in different conditions and decide whether a small change is actually useful.

## Cadence is not a 180 exam

A systematic review found that, at a fixed speed, a higher stride rate generally reduced vertical centre-of-mass excursion, ground reaction force and joint energy absorption — biomechanical factors associated with some running injuries. The included studies were small and methodologically varied, so they do not support “everyone should run at 180 steps per minute”. Treat 180 as a reference, not a target.

A practical approach is to count steps for 30 seconds during easy runs, repeat over several sessions, and watch how the number changes with fatigue, speed and gradient. If you experiment with a higher cadence, change it by about 5% at a time, keep speed constant, and give it two or three weeks before judging comfort. Stop if pain appears.

## Breathing is not a fixed beat

Breathing changes with speed, gradient, fatigue and personal habit. There is no universal “inhale for three steps, exhale for two” that everyone must follow. Forcing a fixed rhythm can increase shoulder and neck tension and add unnecessary effort. The talk test is more useful for intensity: an easy run should allow full sentences; if you can only manage a few words, the effort is already high — slow down or shorten the stride.

Nasal or mouth breathing are both acceptable; the key is meeting ventilation demand. There is no need to force nose-only breathing to look “more professional”. If you are clearly short of breath at an easy effort, or have chest tightness, wheeze or dizziness, stop and seek medical advice.

## Stride length mostly follows speed

Stride length is not a number to “pull” larger by itself. As speed rises, both cadence and stride length usually increase; deliberately overstriding can put the landing farther ahead, increasing braking and joint load. Decide the speed first and let stride length follow, rather than using a long stride to chase speed.

## Uphill and downhill are different skills

Research shows that uphill running usually has a higher step frequency and shorter flight time, with greater hip muscular work. Downhill running has longer flight time, lower step frequency and more eccentric load. Shorten the stride and keep breathing easy uphill; control speed downhill instead of “letting it go” and losing landing control. There is no need to copy a flat-road rhythm onto a climb.

## Surface matters, with limits

One small study compared artificial grass, rubber and concrete and found no significant differences in many joint-motion and loading variables, but higher ankle moments and frontal-plane hip/knee moments on concrete. A single study cannot produce a universal rule, but it is a reminder to reduce intensity and observe your response when the surface is hard and fatigue accumulates.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not diagnose individual form, treat injury or prescribe a “correct” posture for every runner. Persistent pain, a new injury or a history of injury deserves assessment by a qualified medical or sports professional. Technique work cannot replace sleep, load management and recovery.

## Sources and scope

The cadence/load relationship follows a Sports Health systematic review; hill differences follow a Sports Medicine review; surface differences follow a small PLOS ONE study; breathing and intensity judgement follow the CDC talk test. The studies have sample and design limits; this page turns them into an observation framework, not a guarantee.

sources.title: Get running with Couch to 5K
claims: Couch to 5K schedules three runs a week with rest days between, over nine weeks or longer.
It starts with one-minute runs and 1.5-minute walks and builds toward 30 minutes of continuous running.
The NHS advises going at your own pace and speaking to a GP if you are worried about your health before starting.

sources.title: Adult Activity: An Overview
claims: Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity weekly, or an equivalent combination.
Adults also need two days of muscle-strengthening activity each week.
Activity can be spread out and broken up; some activity is better than none.

sources.title: Activity Planner
claims: The planner helps set goals, choose preferred activities and print a weekly tracking plan.
Adults need a mix of moderate aerobic and muscle-strengthening activity.

translations.title: 把跑步变成习惯：从三次轻松跑开始
translations.summary: 可持续的跑步习惯来自可重复的小安排，而不是一次立志跑很多。每周三次、留出休息日、逐步增加，比追求短期强度更容易坚持。
translations.body:
## 先安排能重复的一周

NHS 的 Couch to 5K 以每周三次跑、之间安排休息日开始，九周或更长时间逐步从一分钟跑加一分半走，过渡到连续跑 30 分钟。这个结构的价值不在“九周”这个数字，而在于：有固定频率、有休息、每次只增加一点。

## 目标要能被执行

把“我要开始跑步”改成一个具体的周计划：哪三天、每次多长时间、在哪里、遇到下雨或加班怎么替代。ODPHP 的活动计划工具可以帮助你选择喜欢的活动、设定目标并打印每周记录。一个能在普通工作日完成的计划，比一个只在理想状态成立的计划更可靠。

## 规律比单次强度重要

CDC 建议成年人每周至少 150 分钟中等强度活动，并每周两天力量练习；活动可以分散到一周，也可以拆成小段。对刚开始的人来说，先达到“每周三次、每次轻松完成”比追求一次很长或很快更有意义。轻松跑、跑走交替和步行都算活动。

## 错过一次不等于失败

计划被打断时，下一次从相近但略低的负荷恢复，而不是用一次“补课”把缺的量全部补回来。连续几天疲劳、睡眠变差或出现疼痛时，减少跑量并观察；疼痛持续或影响走路时，参考[疼痛与负荷](/zh-CN/articles/pain-and-load/)，必要时寻求专业评估。

## 记录趋势，不追求完美

记录日期、时长、感受、睡眠和疼痛，而不是只记录配速。每两三周回看一次：什么条件下最容易完成？哪类安排总被跳过？把成功的条件保留下来，把不现实的目标缩小。习惯不是靠意志力硬撑，而是让正确的选择更容易发生。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不给个体化训练计划、不保证减重或成绩，也不替代医生对运动的建议。已有心血管、代谢、骨关节或其他健康问题的人，开始新运动前应咨询合格医疗人员；出现胸痛、晕厥、异常气短等信号应停止运动并寻求紧急帮助。

## 来源与适用范围

三次/周与渐进结构参考 NHS Couch to 5K；成人活动量参考 CDC；目标与每周记录参考 ODPHP 活动计划工具。它们是一般公共卫生和习惯建议，不构成个体化训练处方。

translations.title: Making running a habit: start with three easy runs
translations.summary: A sustainable running habit comes from repeatable small arrangements, not one ambitious week. Three runs a week with rest days and gradual progression is easier to sustain than a short intensity binge.
translations.body:
## Start with a week you can repeat

NHS Couch to 5K starts with three runs a week and rest days between, then builds over nine weeks or longer from one-minute runs with 1.5-minute walks toward 30 minutes of continuous running. The value is not the number “nine”: it is a fixed frequency, planned rest and a small increase at a time.

## Make the goal executable

Turn “I should start running” into a weekly plan: which three days, how long, where, and what happens when it rains or work runs late. The ODPHP activity planner can help choose preferred activities, set goals and print a weekly tracking plan. A plan that works on an ordinary weekday is more reliable than one that only works under ideal conditions.

## Consistency beats one hard session

The CDC recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week and muscle-strengthening activity on two days. Activity can be spread through the week and broken into smaller bouts. For a beginner, “three easy sessions I can complete each week” is more useful than one very long or very fast session. Easy running, run-walk and walking all count as activity.

## A missed session is not failure

When a plan is interrupted, return at a similar but slightly lower load rather than cramming all the missed work into one “make-up” session. If fatigue, sleep or pain persists for several days, reduce running and observe. If pain continues or affects walking, see [pain and load](/en/articles/pain-and-load/) and seek professional assessment when needed.

## Track trends, not perfection

Record date, duration, how it felt, sleep and pain, not only pace. Every two or three weeks, review what conditions made sessions most likely to happen and which arrangements were always skipped. Keep the successful conditions and shrink unrealistic goals. Habits are built by making the right choice easier, not by relying on willpower.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not give an individual training plan, promise weight loss or performance, or replace medical advice about exercise. People with cardiovascular, metabolic, bone/joint or other health conditions should consult a qualified clinician before starting. Stop and seek emergency help for chest pain, fainting or unusual breathlessness.

## Sources and scope

The three-runs-a-week progression follows NHS Couch to 5K; adult activity targets follow the CDC; goal setting and weekly tracking follow the ODPHP activity planner. These are general public-health and habit suggestions, not an individual training prescription.

sources.title: Knee pain and other running injuries
claims: NHS advises buying proper running shoes and getting fitted at a running shop, while noting that expensive shoes are not essential.
Unsupportive or worn-out shoes are listed among factors that can contribute to heel pain.
Do not run while in pain; seek medical or physiotherapy advice when pain is severe, persistent or accompanied by swelling.

sources.title: Association of Shoe Cushioning Perception and Comfort With Injury Risk in Leisure-Time Runners
claims: In a secondary analysis of a randomised trial involving 527 recreational runners, moderate or high perceived heel cushioning was associated with lower injury risk than low cushioning.
Higher overall shoe appreciation was associated with lower injury risk.
The study reports associations, not proof that changing cushioning prevents injury.

sources.title: Ten Essentials
claims: The NPS minimum kit includes navigation, sun protection, clothing, illumination, first aid, fire, repair kit, food, water and water-treatment supplies, and shelter.
Navigation means a map, compass and GPS; a physical map should back up electronic tools.
A headlamp with spare batteries is recommended, and someone should know the route and expected return time.

translations.title: 第一双跑鞋怎么选：合脚、舒适与使用边界
translations.summary: 跑鞋首先解决合脚和舒适，而不是品牌或“最强缓震”。高价不等于更适合；磨损、疼痛和路面变化比营销参数更值得关注。
translations.body:
## 先合脚，再谈技术

选跑鞋的第一步是合脚：脚趾前方留出空间，脚背不被压，走路和慢跑时脚跟不滑动。NHS 建议到跑鞋店试穿并获得合脚建议，但也指出不必花很多钱；高价鞋可能主要在耐用性和轻量上占优，入门者不一定需要。

## 缓震是主观感受，不能只看高低

一项随机试验的二次分析（527 名休闲跑者）发现，较高主观后跟缓震和整体鞋款好感与较低受伤风险相关，但这是关联而非因果，且研究有商业资助背景。它不能证明“换更软的鞋就不会受伤”。选择时以走路、慢跑和变向时的舒适、稳定和合脚为准；不要只看参数或他人推荐。

## 什么时候该换

没有可靠的固定公里数适用于所有人。NHS 把“支撑不足或磨损的鞋”列为脚跟痛的可能因素之一；当你感觉中底明显塌陷、外底磨穿、鞋面失去包裹，或同一双鞋开始让熟悉的动作变得不舒服时，就应考虑更换。记录购买时间和使用场景，比盲目按里程换鞋更实际。

## 越野鞋与公路鞋不是同一件事

公路跑鞋优先考虑在硬质路面上的舒适和稳定；越野跑还要面对泥土、碎石、湿滑和长时间行走。越野鞋的抓地、保护和排水通常以重量和公路脚感为代价。不要把公路鞋当成通用越野鞋，也不要在技术山径上只依赖鞋底。

## 山径装备的最低框架

美国国家公园管理局的“十项必备”是徒步框架：导航、防晒、衣物、照明、急救、取火、维修、食物、饮水与净水、庇护。用于跑步时应按路线长度、天气和撤离条件调整，但头灯与备用电池、基础急救、额外保暖和可靠导航不应因为“只是跑步”而省略。装备不能替代路线判断。

## 本站不提供什么

这里不推荐具体品牌，也不判断某双鞋是否适合你的足型、伤病或比赛目标。持续疼痛、足部结构问题或糖尿病等健康状况，应咨询合格的医疗或足病专业人员；换鞋不是治疗。

## 来源与适用范围

合脚、价格与磨损建议参考 NHS 的跑步损伤页面；缓震感受与受伤风险的关联参考 European Journal of Sport Science 的随机试验二次分析；山径最低装备框架参考美国国家公园管理局。研究结论有局限，不能当作个体化处方。

translations.title: Choosing running shoes: fit, comfort and limits
translations.summary: Running shoes should first fit and feel comfortable, not match a brand or a “maximum cushioning” claim. A higher price does not guarantee a better match; wear, pain and surface matter more than marketing numbers.
translations.body:
## Fit first, technology second

The first test is fit: room in front of the toes, no pressure across the top of the foot, and no heel sliding while walking or jogging. The NHS suggests getting fitted at a running shop but also notes that you do not have to spend a lot; expensive shoes may mainly be more durable or lighter, and beginners may not need them.

## Cushioning is a perception, not a leaderboard

A secondary analysis of a randomised trial involving 527 recreational runners found that higher perceived heel cushioning and overall shoe appreciation were associated with lower injury risk. That is an association, not proof of cause, and the study had a commercial-funding context. It does not prove that “softer shoes prevent injury”. Choose by comfort, stability and fit during walking, easy jogging and changes of direction, not by a spec sheet or someone else’s recommendation.

## When to replace

No fixed mileage applies to everyone. The NHS lists unsupportive or worn-out shoes among possible contributors to heel pain. Consider replacing shoes when the midsole feels collapsed, the outsole is worn through, the upper no longer holds the foot, or a familiar shoe starts making familiar movements uncomfortable. Record purchase date and use case rather than blindly following a mileage rule.

## Trail shoes are not road shoes

Road shoes prioritise comfort and stability on hard surfaces. Trail running adds mud, rock, wet ground and long hiking sections. Grip, protection and drainage usually cost weight and road feel. Do not treat a road shoe as a universal trail shoe, and do not rely on the outsole alone on technical terrain.

## A minimum trail kit

The U.S. National Park Service “Ten Essentials” is a hiking framework: navigation, sun protection, clothing, illumination, first aid, fire, repair kit, food, water and water-treatment supplies, and shelter. Adapt it to the run's length, weather and escape options, but do not omit a headlamp with spare batteries, basic first aid, extra warmth and reliable navigation just because the activity is “only a run”. Gear cannot replace route judgement.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not recommend brands or decide whether a shoe suits your foot shape, injury history or race goal. Persistent pain, structural foot problems or conditions such as diabetes deserve assessment by a qualified medical or podiatry professional; changing shoes is not treatment.

## Sources and scope

Fit, price and wear guidance follows the NHS running-injury page; the cushioning/injury association follows a secondary European Journal of Sport Science analysis of a randomised trial; the minimum trail kit follows the U.S. National Park Service. The evidence has limits and is not an individual prescription.

translations.title: 碳板与先进跑鞋：证据、适用场景和边界
translations.summary: 碳板鞋可能改善部分人的跑步经济性，但研究仍有争议和个体差异。合脚、舒适和可重复训练比“最新科技”更重要。
translations.body:
## 先进鞋款是什么

“先进跑鞋技术”通常指高回弹泡棉加全掌碳纤维板的组合，目的是提高纵向弯曲刚度、改变脚踝和跖趾关节的力学，并可能降低跑步的代谢成本。它不是魔法，也不能替代训练。碳板只是鞋的一部分，泡棉、鞋楦、落差、重量和你的脚型同样影响体验。

## 研究怎么说

一项系统综述和 meta 分析报告，碳板鞋与较低的代谢需求相关，说明部分跑者可能在相同速度下感觉更省力。但作者也指出，碳板本身是否带来代谢收益仍有争议，研究设计、跑步速度和个体反应存在差异，不能把群体平均结果当成每个人都适用的承诺。

生物力学研究也没有发现所有关节负荷都一致下降；不同鞋款和不同跑者的结果可能不同。因此，看到“提升百分之几”的宣传时，先问研究对象、速度、对照鞋款和资助来源。

## 不是所有人都更快

碳板鞋对不同跑者的收益并不相同，配速、步频、足型和适应时间都可能影响结果。对一些人，它可能在比赛或质量课中带来帮助；对另一些人，带来的只是更硬、更不稳定或更贵的感觉。没有证据表明它能预防所有跑步伤病，也不能因为穿了碳板鞋就跳过负荷管理。

如果考虑尝试，先在轻松跑或短质量课中穿几次，观察脚踝、足底、小腿和整体稳定性；不要在比赛日第一次穿新鞋。

## 训练鞋与比赛鞋

训练鞋和比赛鞋可以分开，但“必须轮换”或“必须只穿一双”都没有适用于所有人的证据。轮换可能分散磨损、让泡棉有时间恢复，也可能只是让你更容易管理不同路面和距离。关键是每双鞋都合脚、能稳定完成训练，并记录使用里程和身体反应。

碳板鞋的寿命受泡棉、外底和你的体重、路面影响；没有统一的“多少公里必须更换”数字。外底磨穿、泡棉明显塌陷、鞋面破损或持续不适，都是比里程更直接的信号。

## 什么时候更换

检查外底、鞋头、后跟和鞋面；如果抓地明显下降、泡棉失去弹性、鞋子左右不对称磨损或引起新的疼痛，考虑更换。NHS 的跑步伤病建议也强调合脚、支撑和不要在明显疼痛中继续跑；昂贵或“高科技”不等于适合。

把跑鞋当作变量记录：哪双鞋跑了多少、在什么路面、是否引起不适。比追逐最新款更有用的，是知道哪双鞋能让你的训练稳定重复。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不推荐品牌或具体型号，也不诊断足部、踝关节或膝关节问题。持续疼痛、麻木、肿胀或步态改变，应找合格的医疗或运动专业人士评估。

## 来源与适用范围

碳板鞋的代谢和生物力学证据参考系统综述与 meta 分析；鞋类舒适度与伤病关联参考次要分析；跑鞋和疼痛建议参考 NHS。研究结论有样本和设计限制，本页只给出选择与试验框架。

translations.title: Carbon plates and advanced shoes: evidence, use cases and limits
translations.summary: Carbon-plated shoes may improve running economy for some runners, but the evidence has debate and individual variation. Fit, comfort and repeatable training matter more than the newest technology.
translations.body:
## What advanced footwear means

“Advanced footwear technology” usually combines a highly resilient foam with a full-length carbon-fibre plate. The aim is to increase longitudinal bending stiffness, alter ankle and metatarsophalangeal mechanics, and potentially lower the metabolic cost of running. It is not magic and does not replace training. The plate is only one part of a shoe; foam, last, drop, weight and your foot shape all affect the experience.

## What the research says

A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that carbon-plated shoes were associated with lower metabolic demand, suggesting some runners may find the same speed less costly. The authors also noted that whether the plate itself produces the metabolic benefit remains debated, and that study design, running speed and individual responses vary. A group average is not a promise for every runner.

Biomechanical studies have not shown every joint load falling uniformly; results differ by shoe and runner. When a claim promises a percentage improvement, ask about the study population, speed, comparison shoe and funding.

## Not everyone gets faster

The benefit of carbon plates varies with pace, cadence, foot shape and adaptation. For some runners they may help in a race or quality session; for others they simply feel stiffer, less stable or more expensive. There is no evidence that they prevent every running injury, and wearing them does not remove the need for load management.

If you try a pair, use them first on an easy run or short quality session and watch the ankle, plantar foot, calf and overall stability. Do not wear new shoes for the first time on race day.

## Training shoes and racing shoes

Training and racing shoes can be separated, but neither “always rotate” nor “always use one pair” is supported for everyone. Rotation may spread wear and give foam time to recover; it may also simply help you manage different surfaces and distances. The key is that each pair fits, feels stable and supports repeatable training. Record mileage and body response.

Carbon-plate durability depends on foam, outsole, body weight and surface. There is no universal “replace at X kilometres” number. Worn-through outsole, collapsed foam, a torn upper or persistent discomfort are more useful signals than mileage alone.

## When to replace

Check the outsole, toe box, heel and upper. Consider replacement when grip is clearly reduced, foam has lost its resilience, wear is markedly asymmetric or the shoe is causing new pain. NHS running-injury advice also emphasises fit, support and not running through significant pain; expensive or high-tech does not automatically mean suitable.

Treat shoes as a variable: record which pair you used, on what surface and whether it caused discomfort. That is more useful than chasing the newest model.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not recommend brands or models, or diagnose foot, ankle or knee problems. Persistent pain, numbness, swelling or a change in gait deserves assessment by a qualified medical or sports professional.

## Sources and scope

Metabolic and biomechanical evidence for carbon-plated shoes follows a systematic review and meta-analysis; shoe comfort and injury associations follow a secondary analysis; shoe and pain advice follows the NHS. The studies have sample and design limits; this page provides a selection and testing framework, not a guarantee.

translations.title: 睡眠与恢复：比恢复设备更基础的变量
translations.summary: 睡眠时长和质量会影响训练感受，但不存在适合所有人的完美睡眠模板。连续变差时先降低负荷、固定起床时间，持续失眠则寻求医疗帮助。
translations.body:
## 睡眠不是训练的对立面

睡眠是身体修复、情绪调节和白天功能的基础。NHS 指出，每个人需要的睡眠量不同，大多数成年人需要 7 至 9 小时；持续睡眠问题会影响白天生活，并可能需要医疗建议。训练计划再精细，也不能抵消长期睡眠不足。

## 不要追求一个完美数字

7 至 9 小时是人群范围，不是每晚必须命中的考核线。睡眠需求会随年龄、压力、疾病、旅行和训练量变化。与其盯着某晚的分数，不如看一周趋势：是否经常难以入睡、夜间醒来、起床后仍疲惫，或白天功能受影响。

## 训练安排怎样配合睡眠

当睡眠连续几天变差时，先降低训练量或取消质量课，观察疲劳和情绪是否改善；不要用更多恢复设备或补剂掩盖睡眠问题。固定起床时间、减少睡前刺激、把高强度训练与入睡时间拉开，是常见方向；具体原因和处置应交给医生或睡眠专业人员。

## 比赛前和旅行时

比赛周末的陌生床、早班交通和紧张情绪会影响睡眠。提前安排行程、带熟悉的睡眠用品、避免赛前临时改变全部习惯，比追求“完美睡眠”更实际。若比赛前一晚睡不好，不必用额外咖啡因或陌生补剂补偿；比赛日的熟悉流程更重要。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不诊断失眠、睡眠呼吸暂停或其他睡眠障碍，也不推荐药物、补剂或固定睡眠时长。持续失眠、白天功能明显受损、打鼾伴呼吸暂停或白天突然入睡，应寻求医疗评估；不要在驾驶或操作机械前依赖意志对抗困倦。

## 来源与适用范围

睡眠时长、个体差异和持续失眠的就医提示参考 NHS 的失眠页面。本文提供一般恢复原则，不构成医疗诊断或个体化治疗建议。

translations.title: Sleep and recovery: the variable beneath the gadgets
translations.summary: Sleep duration and quality affect how training feels, but there is no perfect sleep template for everyone. When sleep deteriorates, reduce load and stabilise wake time; persistent insomnia deserves medical help.
translations.body:
## Sleep is not the opposite of training

Sleep supports repair, emotional regulation and daytime function. The NHS notes that sleep needs vary and that most adults need 7 to 9 hours; persistent sleep problems can affect daily life and may need medical advice. No training plan can cancel chronic sleep deprivation.

## Do not chase a perfect number

Seven to nine hours is a population range, not a nightly pass mark. Needs change with age, stress, illness, travel and training load. Rather than fixating on one night's score, look at a week: do you often struggle to fall asleep, wake during the night, wake unrefreshed, or notice daytime impairment?

## Adjust training around sleep

When sleep worsens for several days, reduce volume or drop a quality session and observe fatigue and mood; do not use more recovery gadgets or supplements to mask a sleep problem. A consistent wake time, less stimulation before bed and separating hard training from bedtime are common directions. A clinician or sleep specialist should assess causes and treatment.

## Before races and travel

Unfamiliar beds, early transport and nerves can affect sleep around a race. Plan travel, bring familiar sleep items and avoid changing every habit at the last minute. If the night before a race is poor, do not compensate with extra caffeine or unfamiliar supplements; a familiar race-day routine matters more.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not diagnose insomnia, sleep apnoea or another sleep disorder, and does not recommend medication, supplements or a fixed sleep duration. Persistent insomnia, significant daytime impairment, snoring with breathing pauses or sudden daytime sleepiness should be medically assessed. Do not rely on willpower to fight drowsiness while driving or operating machinery.

## Sources and scope

Sleep duration, individual variation and the advice to seek help for persistent insomnia follow the NHS insomnia page. This is general recovery information, not diagnosis or individual treatment.

translations.title: 力量、交叉训练与减量：把辅助手段放回训练结构
translations.summary: 力量训练和交叉训练是补充，不是替代跑步的捷径；减量也不是完全停跑。关键是维持强度与频率，减少总量，并让恢复和睡眠跟上。
translations.body:
## 力量训练放在哪里

CDC 的成人活动建议每周至少两天进行覆盖主要肌群的力量训练。对跑者来说，力量训练可以帮助维持肌肉和肌腱能力，但“力量训练能否预防所有跑步伤病”的研究证据并不一致；训练负荷、恢复和个体差异同样重要。

刚开始时，每周一到两次、动作简单且能稳定完成，比堆很多动作更实际。尽量把下肢力量安排在不影响关键质量课的位置，或者与轻松跑同一天、间隔数小时；比赛周不要临时加入陌生的大重量训练。

## 交叉训练不是替代跑步

骑车、游泳、椭圆机等低冲击活动可以补充有氧量，在受伤或路面条件差时也有用处。但跑步的专项负荷、落地机制和肌肉协调无法被完全替代；把交叉训练当成“额外加量”而不是恢复，容易让总负荷失控。

如果因疼痛而改用交叉训练，先明确疼痛原因和可承受范围，必要时找医疗或运动专业人士评估。交叉训练不能用来绕过持续加重的疼痛。

## 减量不是完全停跑

一项纳入 14 项研究的系统综述和 meta 分析发现，赛前减量可以改善计时赛和力竭时间表现；常见的有效做法是训练量减少约 41%–60%，同时维持强度和频率，减量期不超过约 21 天。合并赛前超量训练的方案在部分研究中效果更明显。

这并不意味着每个人都要照搬一个百分比。业余跑者可以从一到三周的渐进减量开始：保留少量节奏或短间歇，减少长距离和总里程，优先保证睡眠和饮食。减量期不是“补练”的窗口，突然加课反而会破坏恢复。

## 比赛周怎么排

比赛周的目标是去掉疲劳，不是追求最后一次刺激。把跑量降到平时的较低水平，保留短而轻松的跑动和几次短加速即可；不要尝试新鞋、新补给或新路线。提前处理交通、号码布、装备和补给，把注意力留给比赛本身。

如果减量后反而更疲惫、睡眠变差或出现疼痛，先检查总负荷、压力和健康状态，而不是继续加练。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不提供个体化力量计划、伤病治疗或精确减量百分比。疼痛、持续疲劳、既往伤病和比赛目标冲突时，应由合格的教练、医生或运动专业人士评估。

## 来源与适用范围

成人力量活动建议参考 CDC 和 ODPHP；减量效果与训练量范围参考 PLOS ONE 的系统综述和 meta 分析；跑步负荷与伤病关系的证据边界参考系统综述。研究结论有样本和项目差异，本页只给出安排原则。

translations.title: Strength, cross-training and tapering: fit support work into the plan
translations.summary: Strength and cross-training supplement running rather than replace it; a taper is not complete rest. Keep some intensity and frequency, reduce total volume, and let recovery and sleep catch up.
translations.body:
## Where strength work fits

CDC adult guidance recommends muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week, covering the major muscle groups. For runners, strength work can support muscle and tendon capacity, but the evidence that it prevents every running injury is not uniform; training load, recovery and individual differences also matter.

When starting, one or two sessions a week with a few stable exercises is more useful than a long list. Place lower-body strength where it does not compromise a key quality session, or on an easy day with several hours between sessions. Do not add unfamiliar heavy lifting during race week.

## Cross-training is not a substitute for running

Cycling, swimming and elliptical work can add low-impact aerobic volume and can help when injured or when surfaces are poor. But running-specific load, landing mechanics and coordination cannot be fully replaced. Treating cross-training as extra volume rather than recovery can let total load spiral.

If pain is the reason for switching, first clarify the cause and what you can tolerate, with medical or sports-professional input when needed. Cross-training should not be used to run around steadily worsening pain.

## A taper is not complete rest

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies found that tapering improved time-trial and time-to-exhaustion performance. A common effective pattern reduced training volume by about 41–60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, with tapers lasting up to about 21 days. Some studies found a larger effect when tapering followed pre-taper overload training.

That does not mean copying one percentage. Amateur runners can start with a gradual one-to-three-week taper: keep a little tempo or short intervals, reduce long runs and total mileage, and prioritise sleep and food. The taper is not a window for “catching up” with extra training; adding sessions can spoil the recovery it is meant to create.

## Race week

The goal of race week is to remove fatigue, not to squeeze in one last stimulus. Reduce volume to a comfortable low, keep short easy runs and a few brief accelerations, and avoid new shoes, new fuel or a new route. Sort out transport, bib, kit and nutrition in advance so attention is left for the race.

If tapering leaves you more tired, sleeping badly or in pain, check total load, stress and health rather than adding more training.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not prescribe an individual strength programme, treat injury or give an exact taper percentage. Persistent pain, fatigue, a history of injury or conflicting race goals deserve assessment by a qualified coach, clinician or sports professional.

## Sources and scope

Adult strength guidance follows CDC and ODPHP; taper effects and volume ranges follow the PLOS ONE systematic review and meta-analysis; the limits of running-load and injury evidence follow a systematic review. Study samples and events differ, so this page offers organising principles rather than a guaranteed plan.

translations.title: 节奏跑与间歇跑：把“快”拆成可重复的课
translations.summary: 节奏跑和间歇跑不是每次都跑快，而是用不同强度和恢复时间解决不同问题。先能稳定完成，再谈配速。
translations.body:
## 三种课不是三个配速数字

训练文章常把跑步分成轻松跑、节奏跑和间歇跑，但每个人对应的配速并不相同。同一条“5 分配速”，对一位跑者可能是轻松跑，对另一位已经是高强度。与其背配速表，不如先用谈话测试和主观用力感（RPE）确认今天的强度：轻松跑能说完整句子；节奏跑只能说短句；间歇跑在每段末尾很难说话，但恢复后能重新开始。

配速仍然有用，只是它应该来自你自己的测试和记录，而不是从别人的计划里抄来。

## 轻松跑仍然是主体

高质量的节奏课和间歇课不能替代轻松跑。多数训练框架把大部分时间放在低强度，把少量时间留给质量课；具体比例因目标、经验和恢复而异。如果每一跑都变成“稍微快一点”，轻松跑就失去了恢复作用，质量课也会因为疲劳而做不好。

对刚开始跑步的人，一周一次质量课通常已经足够；有基础的跑者可以安排一到两次，但要保证两次之间至少有一天的轻松跑或休息。质量课之间挤得太近，是常见的“看起来努力、实际练不动”的原因。

## 节奏跑：持续地“ comfortably hard”

节奏跑通常指一段持续时间较长、强度介于轻松跑和比赛配速之间的跑法。不同教练对它的定义不完全相同，所以不必迷信某个名称。可执行的标准是：呼吸明显加快，但还能说短句；动作稳定，不需要靠冲刺维持；结束后感觉“有挑战，但明天还能正常跑”。

一个入门模板是 3 组 8 分钟节奏跑，组间 2 分钟轻松跑；有经验后再延长总时间。把它当作训练课，而不是比赛；如果最后几分钟只能靠咬牙硬撑，说明起步太快或今天状态不适合。

## 间歇跑：短而快，但保留恢复

间歇跑把较快的一段和恢复段交替进行。它的目的不是把每一段都跑成全力，而是让每一段保持动作质量和目标强度，然后在恢复段重新准备好。常见的入门形式是 6 组 3 分钟较快跑，组间 2 分钟轻松跑；也可以使用更短的 1 分钟段落，但总次数要相应调整。

“快”不等于“拼命”。如果动作变形、呼吸无法在恢复段回落，或最后两组明显掉速，就结束这堂课。间歇训练对负荷的刺激很集中，不适合在睡眠不足、疼痛或刚恢复时硬做。

## 怎样安排与调整

先确定一周能重复几次，再把质量课放进计划。节奏跑和间歇跑不要连续安排；质量课前后的日子用轻松跑或休息承接。天气炎热、湿度高或海拔变化时，同一配速的负担会更高，应优先用感受和呼吸判断，而不是坚持原数字。

记录每组的时间、RPE、呼吸和结束时的状态。连续几次同样课程都变得困难，或轻松跑也开始跑不动，先检查睡眠、能量摄入和总负荷，而不是继续加课。

## 本站不提供什么

本页不提供个体化训练计划、精确配速处方或比赛目标保证。疼痛、持续疲劳、既往伤病、心脏或呼吸症状，应由合格的教练、医生或运动专业人士评估；不要用“再坚持一组”掩盖异常信号。

## 来源与适用范围

强度判断参考 CDC 的谈话测试；跑步负荷与伤病关系的证据边界参考系统综述。节奏跑和间歇跑的具体配速、组数和恢复时间因人与目标而异，本页给出的是课程框架，不是统一处方。

translations.title: Tempo and interval sessions: split “fast” into repeatable work
translations.summary: Tempo and interval sessions are not just faster running; they use different intensities and recoveries for different jobs. Complete them consistently before chasing a pace.
translations.body:
## Three session types are not three pace numbers

Training articles often divide running into easy, tempo and interval work, but the pace attached to each label differs between runners. A pace that feels easy for one person may already be hard for another. Instead of copying a pace table, use the talk test and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) to check the day's effort: easy running allows full sentences; tempo running allows only short phrases; intervals make speech difficult by the end of a rep, but recovery should let you start the next one.

Pace still matters, but it should come from your own tests and records, not from someone else's plan.

## Easy running remains the base

Quality sessions do not replace easy running. Most training frameworks place the majority of time at low intensity and reserve a small amount for quality work; the exact distribution depends on the goal, experience and recovery. If every run becomes “a little faster”, easy runs stop doing their recovery job and quality sessions suffer from accumulated fatigue.

For a new runner, one quality session a week is often enough; more experienced runners may use one or two, with an easy day or rest between them. Packing quality sessions too closely together is a common way to look busy while failing to adapt.

## Tempo: sustained “comfortably hard” running

Tempo usually means a sustained block between easy effort and race pace. Definitions vary between coaches, so do not treat the name as a precise physiological boundary. A practical standard is: breathing is clearly faster but short phrases are possible; form stays stable without sprinting; the session feels challenging but leaves you able to run normally the next day.

An entry template is 3 × 8 minutes at tempo with 2 minutes easy between reps; extend the total time only after the session is repeatable. Treat it as training, not a race. If the last minutes require gritting your teeth, the start was too fast or the day was not suitable.

## Intervals: fast reps with enough recovery

Intervals alternate faster work with recovery. The aim is not to make every rep an all-out effort, but to keep form and the intended intensity, then be ready to start again after recovery. A common entry format is 6 × 3 minutes fast with 2 minutes easy; shorter 1-minute reps are also possible with an adjusted total.

“Fast” does not mean “desperate”. End the session if form changes, breathing does not settle during recovery, or the last reps slow sharply. Interval work concentrates load; it is a poor fit for a day with poor sleep, pain or recent illness.

## Fitting the sessions into a week

Decide how many runs you can repeat each week, then place quality work inside that structure. Do not schedule tempo and intervals back-to-back; use easy running or rest around them. Heat, humidity and altitude raise the cost of a given pace, so use breathing and effort before forcing the original number.

Record rep times, RPE, breathing and how you felt afterwards. If the same session keeps getting harder, or easy runs also stop feeling easy, check sleep, energy intake and total load before adding more work.

## What this page does not provide

This page does not prescribe an individual training plan, exact paces or a performance guarantee. Pain, persistent fatigue, previous injury, or heart and breathing symptoms deserve assessment by a qualified coach, clinician or sports professional. Do not use “one more rep” to override an abnormal signal.

## Sources and scope

Intensity judgement follows the CDC talk test; the limits of running-load and injury evidence follow a systematic review. Tempo and interval paces, rep counts and recovery vary by person and goal; this page provides a session framework, not a universal prescription.

sources.title: Ten Essentials
claims: The NPS minimum kit includes navigation, sun protection, clothing, illumination, first aid, fire, repair kit, food, water and water-treatment supplies, and shelter.
Navigation means a map, compass and GPS; a physical map should back up electronic tools.
A headlamp with spare batteries is recommended, and someone should know the route and expected return time.

sources.title: Hiking Safety Tips
claims: Carry enough water for the conditions and turn back before half is gone.
Carry a map, compass, headlamp with spare batteries, whistle, first aid and extra layers.
GPS can be unreliable; carry alternative navigation and do not rely on it alone.
